title: Precision and Accuracy Mastery
description: Edit and refine advanced writing by eliminating dangling modifiers and agreement errors, choosing tense and aspect with precision, using exact dependent prepositions and collocations, and cutting redundancy.
objectives: Identify and correct dangling and misplaced modifiers
Maintain subject–verb agreement in long and complex sentences
Choose tense and aspect to express precise time relations and attitudes
Use dependent prepositions and formal collocations accurately
Edit drafts for concision, redundancy and overall accuracy

lessons.title: Dangling and Misplaced Modifiers
lessons.summary: Make sure every participle clause and modifier attaches to the word it is meant to describe.
objectives: Recognise dangling participle and infinitive clauses
Correct dangling modifiers by changing the subject or expanding the clause
Place limiting modifiers such as only, almost and just precisely
lessons.completionCriteria: Read every section and score at least 70% on the mini quiz.

sections.explanation:
### The rule behind participle clauses
At C1 you learned to write concise participle clauses: *Having finished the report, she went home.* The unwritten rule is that the **implied subject** of the participle must be the **subject of the main clause**. Who finished the report? *She* did, and *she* is the subject of *went*. When the two subjects differ, the modifier has nothing to attach to: it **dangles**.

> ✗ *Walking into the room, the smell of smoke was overwhelming.* (The smell was not walking.)
> ✓ *Walking into the room, I was overwhelmed by the smell of smoke.*

Dangling modifiers are among the most common errors in otherwise advanced writing, and they can produce unintentionally comic images: *Hanging on the wall, Lina admired the portrait.* (Was Lina hanging on the wall?)

### Typical dangling structures
| Type | Dangling ✗ | Corrected ✓ |
|---|---|---|
| present participle | *Driving to work, a deer ran across the road.* | *While I was driving to work, a deer ran across the road.* |
| perfect participle | *Having been delayed for hours, the airline offered passengers a meal.* | *Having been delayed for hours, the passengers were offered a meal.* |
| past participle | *Born in a fishing village, Mara's first novel describes coastal life.* | *Born in a fishing village, Mara describes coastal life in her first novel.* |
| infinitive | *To qualify for the grant, the form must be submitted by March.* | *To qualify for the grant, applicants must submit the form by March.* |
| prepositional + -ing | *After reading the letter, the decision seemed obvious.* | *After reading the letter, she found the decision obvious.* |

### Two ways to fix a dangling modifier
1. **Change the main clause** so that its subject is the doer of the participle: *Walking into the room, **I** was overwhelmed ...*
2. **Expand the modifier** into a full clause with its own subject: ***As I walked** into the room, the smell of smoke was overwhelming.*

Note that a possessive does not rescue the sentence: in *Born in a fishing village, Mara's novel ...*, the subject is *novel*, not *Mara*.

### Accepted exceptions
Some participles have become prepositions or sentence adverbials and do not need a matching subject: *Considering the weather, the turnout was good. / Generally speaking, ... / Judging by his tone, ... / Given the circumstances, ... / Assuming that ...*. These are standard.

### Misplaced limiting modifiers
Words such as *only, almost, just, even, nearly* modify the element they precede in careful writing:
- *Only Tomas passed the exam.* (no one else passed)
- *Tomas passed only the exam.* (he passed nothing else)
- *She almost failed every module* (she passed them all, narrowly) vs *She failed almost every module.*

In speech, *only* is often placed before the verb and stress clarifies the meaning, but in formal writing place it directly before the element it limits.

questions.prompt: Which sentence avoids a dangling modifier?
questions.instructions: For each sentence, ask who is doing the action in the opening clause. Is that person or thing the subject of the main clause?
options: Walking into the room, the smell of smoke was overwhelming.
Walking into the room, I was overwhelmed by the smell of smoke.
Having finished the report, the computer was switched off.
After reading the letter, the decision seemed obvious.
questions.explanation: In the second sentence, I is both the person walking and the subject of the main clause. In the others, the main subjects (the smell, the computer, the decision) cannot walk, finish a report or read a letter.

questions.prompt: Correct the dangling modifier. You may change the main clause or expand the opening clause.
questions.sentence: Having been delayed for six hours, the airline offered the passengers a free meal.
answers: Having been delayed for six hours, the passengers were offered a free meal by the airline.
Having been delayed for six hours, the passengers were offered a free meal.
Because the passengers had been delayed for six hours, the airline offered them a free meal.
As the passengers had been delayed for six hours, the airline offered them a free meal.
Since the passengers had been delayed for six hours, the airline offered them a free meal.
Because they had been delayed for six hours, the passengers were offered a free meal by the airline.
The airline offered the passengers a free meal because they had been delayed for six hours.
The airline offered the passengers a free meal as they had been delayed for six hours.
The passengers, having been delayed for six hours, were offered a free meal by the airline.
The passengers had been delayed for six hours, so the airline offered them a free meal.
questions.explanation: The passengers, not the airline, were delayed. Either make the passengers the subject (the passengers were offered ...) or turn the opening into a full clause with its own subject (Because the passengers had been delayed ...).

questions.prompt: Which segment must change so that the opening clause attaches to the right subject?
segments: Born in a small fishing village,
questions.explanation: Mara, not her novel, was born in the village. Because the subject is novel, the participle dangles; the possessive Mara's does not make Mara the subject. Rewriting as 'Mara, in her first novel, describes ...' fixes it.

questions.prompt: Rewrite the sentence so that the modifier no longer dangles.
questions.sentence: Walking along the beach, a crab bit my toe.
questions.cue: Keep 'Walking along the beach,' and make 'I' the subject of the main clause.
answers: Walking along the beach, I was bitten on the toe by a crab.
Walking along the beach, I was bitten on my toe by a crab.
Walking along the beach, I was bitten by a crab on the toe.
Walking along the beach, I was bitten by a crab on my toe.
Walking along the beach, I got bitten on the toe by a crab.
Walking along the beach, I got bitten on my toe by a crab.
Walking along the beach, I had my toe bitten by a crab.
Walking along the beach, I got my toe bitten by a crab.
questions.explanation: The crab was not walking along the beach; I was. A passive (I was bitten) or have/get something done structure (I had my toe bitten) makes I the subject.

questions.prompt: Which sentence clearly means that nobody except Tomas passed the exam?
options: Only Tomas passed the exam.
Tomas only passed the exam.
Tomas passed only the exam.
Tomas passed the only exam.
questions.explanation: Placing only directly before Tomas limits the subject: no one else passed. 'Tomas passed only the exam' means he passed nothing else; 'Tomas only passed the exam' suggests he merely passed (rather than excelled) or passed nothing else; 'the only exam' means there was a single exam.

questions.prompt: Select ALL the sentences that contain a dangling modifier.
options: After finishing the exam, the students were allowed to leave.
After finishing the exam, the room was quickly emptied.
Using a new method, the researchers obtained clearer results.
Using a new method, the results became much clearer.
Hanging on the wall, Lina admired the portrait.
Lina admired the portrait hanging on the wall.
questions.explanation: A room cannot finish an exam, results cannot use a method, and Lina was presumably not hanging on the wall. In the other sentences, the opening modifier correctly refers to the subject (the students, the researchers) or the participle follows the noun it describes (the portrait hanging on the wall).

lessons.title: Agreement in Complex Sentences
lessons.summary: Keep subjects and verbs in agreement when long noun phrases, correlatives and quantifiers intervene.
objectives: Identify the head noun of a long subject
Apply agreement rules for neither ... nor, as well as, each and a number of
Use plural Latin and Greek nouns such as criteria and phenomena correctly
lessons.completionCriteria: Read every section and score at least 70% on the mini quiz.

sections.explanation:
### Find the head noun
In long subjects, the verb agrees with the **head noun**, not with the noun nearest to the verb. Post-modifiers (prepositional phrases, relative clauses, participle phrases) do not change the number of the head.

> *The **results** of the survey conducted among teachers in three provinces **suggest** a growing problem.*
> *The **list** of candidates who have applied for the posts **has** been published.*

A reliable test: strip away everything between the head noun and the verb (*The results ... suggest*; *The list ... has*).

### Phrases that do not add subjects
*As well as, together with, along with, in addition to, including* and *rather than* introduce extra information but do **not** make the subject plural:
> *The **director**, together with her two assistants, **is** expected to attend.*

Compare with *and*, which does create a plural subject: *The director and her assistants **are** expected to attend.*

### Correlatives and proximity
With *either ... or* and *neither ... nor*, the verb agrees with the **nearer** subject:
> *Neither the minister nor his **advisers were** available.*
> *Either the advisers or the **minister is** going to respond.*

If the result sounds awkward, put the plural subject second.

### Quantifiers and number expressions
| Expression | Verb | Example |
|---|---|---|
| each / every + singular noun | singular | Every proposal **has** been reviewed. |
| each of + plural noun | singular | Each of the proposals **has** been reviewed. |
| a number of + plural noun | plural | A number of applicants **have** withdrawn. |
| the number of + plural noun | singular | The number of applicants **has** risen. |
| a series / a range / a variety of | usually singular in formal style | A series of meetings **was** held. |
| plenty of / a lot of / most of | agrees with the noun | Most of the money **was** spent; most of the books **were** lost. |

### Plural forms from Latin and Greek
Several academic nouns keep classical plurals: *criterion → criteria, phenomenon → phenomena, hypothesis → hypotheses, analysis → analyses, thesis → theses*. *The criteria **are** unclear* (not *is*). *Data* is used with both singular and plural verbs in modern English (*the data is / are*), so follow your institution's style guide; *criteria* and *phenomena*, however, should always be plural.

### Other traps
- **Inverted subjects** follow the verb: *Among the guests **were** two former ministers.*
- **What-clefts**: *What we need **is** more volunteers* (singular is standard in formal writing).
- **Titles and amounts** are treated as single units: *Three years **is** a long time. / 'Tales of the Harbour' **is** her best book.*

sections.summary: Verbs agree with the head noun of the subject, not the nearest noun. As well as and together with do not create plural subjects; neither ... nor and either ... or agree with the nearer subject. Each (of) is singular, a number of is plural and the number of is singular. Criteria and phenomena are plurals.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct verb form for each gap.
questions.instructions: The number of focuses on a single figure; a number of means 'several'.
questions.text: The number of applicants ___ risen sharply this year, and a number of them ___ from overseas.
questions.explanation: The number of + plural noun takes a singular verb because the head is number (has risen). A number of means several and takes a plural verb (a number of them come).

questions.prompt: Find the segment with an agreement error.
questions.explanation: The head noun of the subject is results (plural), so the verb must be suggest. Survey, teachers and provinces are inside post-modifiers and do not control agreement.

questions.text: The director, together with her two assistants, ___ expected to attend the hearing.
answers: is
was
questions.explanation: Together with introduces additional information but does not make the subject plural. The head is director, so the verb is is (or was in a past context).

questions.prompt: Which sentence is correct in formal written English?
options: Neither the minister nor his advisers was available for comment.
Neither the minister nor his advisers were available for comment.
Neither the minister or his advisers were available for comment.
Neither of the minister and his advisers were available for comment.
questions.explanation: With neither ... nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject (advisers → were). Neither must pair with nor, not or, and 'neither of' is followed by a plural noun phrase, not two coordinated nouns.

questions.prompt: Correct the agreement error.
questions.sentence: Each of the proposals have been carefully considered by the panel.
answers: Each of the proposals has been carefully considered by the panel.
questions.explanation: Each is the head of the subject, so the verb is singular: has been considered.

answers: The criteria used in this study are unclear.
The criteria used in this study are not clear.
The criteria used in this research are unclear.
The criteria used in this research are not clear.
The criteria used in this study were unclear.
The criteria used in this study were not clear.
The criteria used in this research were unclear.
The criteria used in this research were not clear.

lessons.title: Subtle Choices of Tense and Aspect
lessons.summary: Choose tense and aspect to express exact time relations, temporariness and attitude.
objectives: Choose between present perfect and past simple according to time frame
Use progressive aspect for temporariness, irritation and politeness
Use future perfect, future progressive and past perfect where they are required
lessons.completionCriteria: Read every section and score at least 70% on the mini quiz.

sections.explanation:
### Tense and aspect
**Tense** locates an action in time (past, present). **Aspect** shows how the speaker views it: as complete (simple), in progress (progressive) or connected to a later point (perfect). At C2, errors rarely involve form; they involve **choosing** the form that best expresses the intended meaning.

### Present perfect vs past simple
The present perfect links the past to **now**; the past simple places an action in a **finished** time frame.

| Time frame | Tense | Example |
|---|---|---|
| unfinished (so far, this week, since 2015, yet) | present perfect | I **have sent** three emails so far. |
| finished (yesterday, in 2019, when I was a child) | past simple | I **sent** three emails yesterday. |
| "the first/second time" + now | present perfect | It's the third time the printer **has broken** this week. |
| news: headline fact, then details | present perfect, then past simple | The minister **has resigned**. She **announced** her decision at noon. |

### Progressive for meaning, not just duration
The progressive adds meanings beyond "in progress":
- **temporariness**: *I'm living with my aunt until my flat is ready.*
- **irritation** with *always/constantly/forever*: *He's always borrowing my charger without asking.*
- **politeness/tentativeness**: *I was wondering if you could help.* / *I'm hoping you can join us.*
- **change or development**: *The climate is becoming more unpredictable.*

### Stative verbs with a change of meaning
Stative verbs (*think, have, see, taste, be*) are normally simple, but some have dynamic meanings that allow the progressive:

| Stative (simple) | Dynamic (progressive possible) |
|---|---|
| I **think** it's a good idea. (opinion) | I'm **thinking** of applying. (considering) |
| The soup **tastes** salty. (quality) | The chef is **tasting** the soup. (action) |
| She **has** a car. (possession) | She's **having** lunch. (activity) |
| He **is** rude. (character) | He's **being** rude. (behaviour now) |

### Future perfect and future progressive
- **Future perfect** = completed before a future point: *By the time the inspectors arrive, we **will have completed** all the checks.*
- **Future progressive** = in progress at a future point: *At this time tomorrow, I'**ll be sitting** on a train.* It also expresses a neutral future plan: *Will you **be using** the car tonight?* (less pushy than *Will you use ...?*)

### When the past perfect is required
Use the past perfect when the order of past events is not otherwise clear, especially after verbs of realising, discovering and reporting: *When the auditors arrived, the accountant realised that someone **had deleted** the files.* With *before/after*, the sequence is clear, so the past simple is often enough.

### Present perfect progressive vs simple
The progressive emphasises **activity and duration**, the simple emphasises **result or quantity**: *I've been writing all morning* vs *I've written four pages.* With *since/for*, both are often possible for long-term situations: *She has worked / has been working here since 2015.*

mistakes.why: Yesterday is a finished time frame and requires the past simple.

sections.summary: Choose the present perfect for unfinished time frames and the past simple for finished ones. Use progressive aspect for temporariness, irritation, politeness and change, and allow it with stative verbs only when they have a dynamic meaning. Use the future perfect for completion before a future point, and the past perfect when an earlier past event must be distinguished.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct form: "I ___ three emails to the council so far, but nobody has replied."
questions.instructions: 'So far' means 'from the past until now'. Is the time frame finished or unfinished?
options: have sent
sent
had sent
am sending
questions.explanation: So far marks an unfinished time frame reaching up to now, so the present perfect (have sent) is required. The past simple sent cannot combine with so far, had sent needs a past reference point, and am sending does not express a completed number of emails.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct future form for each gap.

questions.explanation: By the time + future point requires the future perfect for an action finished before that point: will have completed. 'At this time tomorrow' refers to an action in progress at a future moment, so the future progressive is needed: will be sitting.

questions.prompt: Complete with the correct form of 'work'.

answers: I have been learning the cello for three years.
I've been learning the cello for three years.

I've been learning the cello for the past three years.

I have been learning to play the cello for three years.
I have been playing the cello for three years.

lessons.title: Precise Prepositions and Formal Collocations
lessons.summary: Use exact dependent prepositions and formal collocations that mark polished writing.
objectives: Use dependent prepositions after formal adjectives, verbs and nouns
Distinguish confusable patterns such as consist of / comprise / be composed of
Use formal collocations such as contingent on and tantamount to
lessons.completionCriteria: Read every section and score at least 70% on the mini quiz.

sections.explanation:
### Why prepositions matter at C2
Dependent prepositions are often unpredictable: we are *capable **of*** something but *able **to*** do it; a plan is *contingent **on*** funding, but *dependent **on*** it too; a remark can be *tantamount **to*** an insult. Errors here rarely block comprehension, but they are highly visible to examiners and editors, and they distinguish C2 writing from C1.

### Formal adjectives with fixed prepositions
| Adjective | Preposition | Example |
|---|---|---|
| conducive | to | Quiet rooms are conducive to concentration. |
| tantamount | to | His silence was tantamount to an admission. |
| impervious | to | She seemed impervious to criticism. |
| oblivious | to / of | He was oblivious to the danger. |
| contingent | on / upon | The offer is contingent on references. |
| prone | to | The valley is prone to flooding. |
| fraught | with | The journey was fraught with danger. |
| devoid | of | The speech was devoid of substance. |
| rich | in | The region is rich in minerals. |
| capable | of | Are they capable of winning? |

### Consist, comprise and compose
These verbs describe parts and wholes and are frequently confused:
- **consist of** (whole → parts): *The committee **consists of** twelve members.*
- **comprise** (whole → parts, no preposition): *The committee **comprises** twelve members.*
- **be composed of / be made up of**: *The committee **is composed of** twelve members.*
- **consist in** (formal) = have as its essential feature: *Happiness consists in contentment.*

*Comprises of* is an error. *Is comprised of* is very common but criticised by many editors; in exams and careful writing, use *consists of*, *comprises* or *is composed of*.

### Prepositions with nouns and verbs
- *an increase **in** prices* (the thing that rises) vs *an increase **of** 5%* (the amount)
- *a solution **to*** a problem; *the key **to*** success; *an approach **to*** teaching
- *meet **with** opposition / approval*; *comply **with** the rules*; *account **for** a difference*
- *insist **on***, *object **to** + -ing*, *refrain **from** + -ing*

### Different from / to / than
*Different from* is accepted everywhere; *different to* is common in British English; *different than* is common in American English. In formal international writing, *different from* is the safest choice.

### Strategy
Record new formal words in a phrase, never alone: not *conducive* but *conducive to learning*. When editing, check every adjective + preposition pair in a learner's or collocation dictionary, especially in high-stakes writing.

sections.summary: Formal adjectives, verbs and nouns take fixed prepositions: conducive to, tantamount to, contingent on, impervious to, oblivious to/of, prone to, fraught with, devoid of, rich in. Use consist of, comprise (no preposition) or be composed of for parts and wholes. Learn every formal word together with its preposition.

questions.prompt: Choose the correct option: "The selection committee ___ twelve members from four departments."
questions.instructions: Which verb describes a whole and its parts, and which preposition (if any) does it take?
options: consists of
comprises of
consists in
is comprised by
questions.explanation: Consist of introduces the parts of a whole. Comprise takes no preposition, so 'comprises of' is wrong; consist in means 'have as its essential feature'; and 'is comprised by' is not standard.

questions.prompt: Drag the correct prepositions into the gaps.
questions.text: The final payment is contingent ___ the board's approval, and failing to deliver the goods would be tantamount ___ a breach of contract.
answers: on
to
questions.explanation: Contingent is followed by on (or upon), and tantamount is always followed by to. With, of and for do not combine with these adjectives.

questions.prompt: Complete with the correct preposition.
questions.text: Constant interruptions and noise are hardly conducive ___ deep concentration.
answers: to
questions.explanation: Conducive is always followed by to: conducive to concentration, conducive to learning.

questions.prompt: Find the segment with a preposition error.
segments: with the tension in the room
questions.correction: to the tension in the room
questions.explanation: Oblivious takes to (or of): oblivious to the tension. 'Continued to tell' is correct.

questions.prompt: Select ALL the sentences with the correct dependent preposition.
options: The success of the plan is contingent on public support.
Her behaviour was tantamount to a confession.
The region is rich of natural resources.
He is totally impervious to criticism.
The team is capable for winning the league.
The village is prone with flooding.
questions.explanation: Contingent on, tantamount to and impervious to are correct. The errors should be rich in, capable of winning and prone to flooding.

questions.prompt: Rewrite the sentence in a more formal style using the word in the cue.
questions.sentence: Whether the project succeeds depends on the weather.
answers: The success of the project is contingent on the weather.
The success of the project is contingent upon the weather.
The project's success is contingent on the weather.
The project's success is contingent upon the weather.
Whether the project succeeds is contingent on the weather.
Whether the project succeeds is contingent upon the weather.
questions.explanation: Be contingent on/upon is a formal equivalent of depend on. Nominalising 'whether the project succeeds' as 'the success of the project' adds further formality.

lessons.title: Editing and Refining Advanced Writing
lessons.summary: Edit drafts for concision, redundancy and accuracy, integrating structures from across the C levels.
objectives: Eliminate redundancy and wordiness in advanced writing
Proofread systematically for the errors studied in this unit
Combine C-level structures accurately when revising sentences
lessons.completionCriteria: Read every section and score at least 70% on the mini quiz.

sections.explanation:
### Editing as a skill
Proficient writers rarely produce perfect first drafts; they **revise**. Editing at C2 means improving clarity and precision without losing meaning. It involves three passes: **content and structure** (is the argument clear?), **style** (is it concise and appropriate in register?) and **accuracy** (are grammar, collocation and punctuation correct?).

### Redundancy
A **redundant** expression repeats an idea already contained in another word. Common examples:

| Redundant | Concise |
|---|---|
| past history | history |
| free gift | gift |
| end result | result |
| advance planning | planning |
| merge together | merge |
| revert back | revert |
| completely unanimous | unanimous |
| in my personal opinion, I think | in my opinion / I think |
| each and every | each / every |

### Wordiness
Wordy phrases can usually be replaced by one or two words:
- *due to the fact that* → **because**
- *in spite of the fact that* → **although**
- *at this moment in time* → **now / currently**
- *in the event that* → **if**
- *has the ability to* → **can**
- *it is important to note that* → (often delete)
- *a large number of* → **many**

Concision is not the same as brevity: do not delete information. *Because the train was late, we missed the scheduled meeting* is concise; *The train was late* is merely short.

### An accuracy checklist
When proofreading, check the specific errors that proficient writers still make:
1. **Modifiers**: does every participle clause attach to the correct subject? (Lesson 1)
2. **Agreement**: does the verb agree with the head noun? (Lesson 2)
3. **Tense and aspect**: does each verb form match its time frame? (Lesson 3)
4. **Prepositions and collocations**: conducive to, comprise without of, heavy rain? (Lesson 4 and Unit 4)
5. **Parallelism**: are listed items in the same form? (Unit 6)
6. **Inversion and fronting**: is the auxiliary in the right place after *Not until*, *So severe*, *Only after*? (C1 Unit 1, C2 Unit 1)
7. **Register**: are informal words creeping into formal text? (Unit 5)

### Integrating C-level structures
Editing is also the moment to *upgrade* sentences: combine short sentences with participle clauses, use nominalisation for formality, add an inversion or cleft for emphasis, and hedge claims appropriately. But each structure must be accurate: an elegant inversion with the wrong auxiliary is worse than a plain sentence.

### Reading aloud
Reading your text aloud, or using a text-to-speech tool, helps you notice missing words, awkward rhythm and over-long sentences. Many professional editors also leave a draft for a day before the final check, so that they read what is actually on the page rather than what they intended to write.

grammar.pattern: Not until + clause + auxiliary + subject + verb

grammar.note: Check the inverted auxiliary when editing.

mistakes.wrong: In my personal opinion, I think the policy is basically unnecessary.
mistakes.right: In my opinion, the policy is unnecessary.
mistakes.why: Personal, I think and basically repeat or weaken the idea; one opinion marker is enough.

mistakes.wrong: The two firms merged together last year.
mistakes.right: The two firms merged last year.
mistakes.why: Merge already means come together, so together is redundant.

mistakes.wrong: Due to the fact that funding was cut, the project was cancelled.
mistakes.right: Because funding was cut, the project was cancelled.
mistakes.why: Due to the fact that is a wordy equivalent of because.

mistakes.wrong: Not until the report was published the errors were noticed.
mistakes.right: Not until the report was published were the errors noticed.
mistakes.why: A fronted Not until clause requires inversion in the main clause.

sections.summary: Edit in three passes: content and structure, style, and accuracy. Remove redundancy (past history, free gift, merge together) and wordiness (due to the fact that → because) without deleting information. Use a checklist covering modifiers, agreement, tense, prepositions, parallelism, inversion and register, and upgrade sentences only with structures you can use accurately.

reviewCards.front: past history / free gift / end result

reviewCards.back: concise keeps all the information in fewer words; short may lose information

questions.prompt: Which phrase is redundant?
questions.instructions: Look for a phrase in which the adjective repeats an idea already contained in the noun.
options: past history
recent history
brief history
family history
questions.explanation: History is by definition in the past, so past adds nothing. Recent, brief and family all add new information about the history.

questions.prompt: Rewrite the sentence concisely, removing all redundancy but keeping the meaning.
questions.sentence: In my personal opinion, I think that the new policy is basically unnecessary.
answers: In my opinion, the new policy is unnecessary.
I think the new policy is unnecessary.
I think that the new policy is unnecessary.
In my view, the new policy is unnecessary.
I believe the new policy is unnecessary.
I believe that the new policy is unnecessary.
I consider the new policy unnecessary.
I consider the new policy to be unnecessary.
The new policy is, in my opinion, unnecessary.
The new policy is, in my view, unnecessary.
questions.explanation: In my personal opinion and I think both mark the statement as an opinion, and personal adds nothing to my. Basically is a filler word. One opinion marker is enough.

questions.prompt: Find the segment that contains a redundant word.
questions.explanation: A gift is by definition free, so free gift is redundant, although it is common in advertising. In careful writing, a gift is sufficient.

questions.prompt: Put the fragments in order to form a polished sentence from a review panel's report.
acceptedAnswers: Having reviewed the evidence, the panel concluded that the original findings remained broadly valid, though flawed.
questions.explanation: The perfect participle clause comes first and attaches to the subject the panel (who reviewed the evidence). The concessive insertion though flawed sits between the subject of the that-clause (the original findings) and its verb (remained).

questions.prompt: Which version is the most concise while keeping all the information?
questions.context: Original: "Due to the fact that the train was late, we were unable to attend the meeting that had been scheduled."
options: Because the train was late, we missed the scheduled meeting.
Due to the fact of the train being late, we could not attend.
The train was late.
Because of the train was late, we missed the meeting.
questions.explanation: The first option keeps all the information in fewer words. The second is still wordy and drops the meeting, the third loses the consequence, and the fourth is ungrammatical (because of must be followed by a noun phrase, not a clause).

questions.prompt: Choose the correct form for each gap.
questions.text: Not until the final draft ___ submitted did the editor notice that the data ___ incorrectly labelled from the start.
questions.explanation: The Not until clause itself is not inverted and needs a passive: the final draft was submitted. The labelling happened before the editor noticed, so the past perfect passive had been is required; has been and have been clash with the past narrative.

unitTestQuestions.sentence: While cooking dinner, the smoke alarm went off.
answers: While I was cooking dinner, the smoke alarm went off.
While we were cooking dinner, the smoke alarm went off.
While she was cooking dinner, the smoke alarm went off.
While he was cooking dinner, the smoke alarm went off.
While they were cooking dinner, the smoke alarm went off.
While cooking dinner, I heard the smoke alarm go off.
While cooking dinner, we heard the smoke alarm go off.
While cooking dinner, I set off the smoke alarm.
The smoke alarm went off while I was cooking dinner.
The smoke alarm went off while we were cooking dinner.
unitTestQuestions.explanation: The smoke alarm was not cooking dinner. Either expand the opening into a full clause with its own subject (While I was cooking dinner) or make the cook the subject of the main clause (While cooking dinner, I heard ...).

unitTestQuestions.prompt: Choose the correct verb for each gap.
unitTestQuestions.text: A list of the shortlisted candidates' names ___ been posted on the noticeboard, but there ___ several spelling errors in it.
unitTestQuestions.explanation: The head noun of the first subject is list (singular), so has been posted. In the there-clause, the verb agrees with the following noun phrase several spelling errors (plural), so are.

unitTestQuestions.prompt: Complete with the correct form of 'break' (the particle 'down' is already given).
unitTestQuestions.text: This is the third time the printer ___ down this week.
answers: has broken
unitTestQuestions.explanation: 'This is the first/second/third time' is followed by the present perfect: has broken down.

unitTestQuestions.prompt: Find the segment with a preposition error.
unitTestQuestions.explanation: The fixed collocation is meet with opposition (or approval, resistance). In the passive it remains was met with, not was met by.

unitTestQuestions.prompt: Which sentence is correct and free of redundancy?
options: The two companies merged together in 2019.
The two companies merged in 2019.
The two companies were merged together each other in 2019.
The two companies merged with each other together in 2019.
unitTestQuestions.explanation: Merge already means join together, so together is redundant. The third and fourth options are also ungrammatical.

unitTestQuestions.prompt: Put the words in order to form a sentence with inversion.
unitTestQuestions.explanation: Only after + clause is fronted, so the main clause is inverted: was the report published. The subordinate clause (the figures had been verified) keeps normal word order and uses the past perfect passive for the earlier event.
